2. Read the head: the first 36 lines hold manifest, essence and routing (Read limit=36, or jq '{manifest, essence, routing}' pelican-bike.metadump.json).
3. Pick the route for your job and run its jq: jq '<routing[i].jq>' pelican-bike.metadump.json
4. Also pull the anti-keywords and review prompts (checks) for your scope: jq '.anti_keywords, .checks' pelican-bike.metadump.json
5. Look up any term (lowercase): jq '.index["<term>"]' pelican-bike.metadump.json  -> hits give id + path; not_meant lists senses to avoid.
6. Grep works too: every entry is one line, so grep -n '<word>' pelican-bike.metadump.json returns whole entries.

7. When you have built something that renders, look at it before you finish: python3 <SKILL>/scripts/look.py <your file.html> screenshots it at desktop and phone widths, then plays it (clicks, types, slides, drags and tabs through everything) and lists what breaks along the way and what the page said. llm_brief.text:
On the table: the user's words, quoted: an SVG animation of a pelican riding a bike, which is motion inside one vector file rather than a still. Pelican cues: a long flat bill, a throat pouch that hangs from the lower jaw, a short S-curved neck that carries the head forward of the chest, a chunky body with a wing folded along its side and the tips trailing past the tail base. Bicycle cues: two equal wheel rings, a diamond frame triangle, cranks at the bottom bracket with a chainring and a rear cog, a saddle on a seat post, bars on the head tube. Contacts: the saddle under the body, two webbed feet on the pedal circles, a wing tip on a grip. Pivots: each wheel turns about its own hub, with transform-box fill-box and transform-origin set on the hub; the cranks use an explicit viewBox origin at the bottom bracket, with transform-box view-box and that point given in viewBox coordinates; the wing shoulder near the front of the back; the frame and body need none. Motion: wheels turning at a steady rate, cranks tracing circles with each foot riding its pedal, the body dipping once per stroke while the neck and bill lag, wing tips trailing. Deep cuts: overlapping follow-through, arcs for the neck sweep, a small lean as anticipation before a push, CSS keyframes that keep each pivot in the style block against SMIL animateTransform that keeps it in the markup, and a reduced-motion media query that can still the ride.

Ways in: a pelican seated on the saddle and pedaling, the whole bicycle in view; a pelican perched forward on the handlebars with its feet on the pedals; a pelican low over a slim racer with drop bars; a pelican upright on a cargo bike with a crate over the front wheel; a pelican upright on a townie bicycle with a wicker basket on the bars and mudguards over both wheels.

Dials: loop length as a spread, 1.2 s, 2.4 s or 4.8 s, each a whole number of crank turns so the frame at the end matches the start; the short one reads busy, the long one calm. Body bob as one eased dip per stroke or two stepped dips for a punchier push; wheels and cranks stay linear in both. Head-to-body and wing-to-body proportions, cadence and wheel speed are open, so any value is an illustration.

Worn paths: the usual move is a white duck blob with a bill; fresher: a long bill with a hanging throat pouch and an S-curved neck, or a brown-grey body with a white head. The usual move is wheels spinning about the frame centre; fresher: each wheel turns about its own hub while the frame rides along. The usual move is a rider hovering above the seat; fresher: the seat stays on the saddle all loop and the torso bobs with each stroke. The usual move is feet off the pedals; fresher: feet planted on the pedals, knees rising and falling with each crank turn. The usual move is a motorbike frame with a fuel tank; fresher: a diamond bicycle frame with a chainring, a rear sprocket and a saddle on a seatpost. The usual move is a GIF or a raster sprite; fresher: one vector SVG with the motion in CSS keyframes, SMIL or a script. The usual move is a jump at the loop seam; fresher: a last keyframe equal to the first, with the wheels ending on a full turn.

Open: whether the loop repeats or plays once, whether the ground scrolls under a fixed rider, and the background all stay open; the pedal cadence and wheel speed at a riding pace are not in a fetched source.

k-rider-on-saddle.text: Does the seat stay under the pelican for the whole loop, with the body dipping above it rather than hovering?

test.spec: in sampled frames at 0, 25, 50 and 75 percent the saddle shape touches the body's underside and no gap opens between them

k-wheel-on-hub.text: Does each wheel turn about its own hub, with the frame and the spokes riding along?

test.spec: the hub stays fixed in each frame while the spokes sweep around it; the frame does not orbit the wheel centre

k-feet-on-pedals.text: Does each foot stay on its pedal as the crank turns?

test.spec: each foot lies on the circle its pedal traces around the bottom bracket in every sampled frame

k-loop-seam.text: Does the loop close without a jump, with the last frame matching the first?

test.spec: the 0% and 100% keyframes give the same transform and opacity on every animated group

k-pelican-readable.text: Does the bird read as a pelican at a glance, with the long bill and the hanging pouch visible?

test.spec: a viewer names the bird from one second on the first frame, without a prompt

k-bicycle-readable.text: Does the bicycle read from two equal wheel rings and a diamond frame triangle?

test.spec: the two wheels match in size and the frame shows a sloping triangle with a saddle on a seat post

k-not-motorbike.text: Does the vehicle read as a pedal bicycle with a chainring, rather than a motorbike or a scooter?

test.spec: no fuel tank, engine or handlebar throttle appears in the drawing

k-crank-layout.text: Do the cranks and chainring turn about the bottom bracket, below the seat?

test.spec: the crank centre sits below the seat tube, at the same point the pedals orbit

k-vector-only.text: Is the file one vector document that plays in a browser with no bitmap frames?

test.spec: open the file alone in a browser: no img, image or video element, and no external request

k-pivot-set.text: Does every rotating part set its own pivot, with the frame and body left without one?

test.spec: each element with a rotate keyframe carries transform-origin and transform-box; the frame group carries neither

k-pixel-pivot.text: Where a pivot is given in pixels, does it match the viewBox coordinates?

test.spec: the hub point in pixels equals the hub point in viewBox units at the drawn scale

k-reduced-motion.text: Does the ride respond to a reduced-motion preference by stilling or slowing the wheels, with the pelican still reading?

test.spec: emulate prefers-reduced-motion: reduce; the wheels stop or slow, and the pose still reads as a pelican seated on a bicycle

k-viewbox-fit.text: Does the drawing stay inside one fixed viewBox and scale to the page width without clipping the wheels?

test.spec: at 390 px wide both wheels and the bill stay inside the frame, with no horizontal scroll

k-animated-on-load.text: Does the file animate on load, rather than sitting as a still picture?

test.spec: two frames one second apart differ in the wheel spokes and the body position

k-keyframes-used.text: Are the wheel and crank motions written as keyframes that run linear and infinite?

test.spec: wheel rotate keyframes read 0 to 360 degrees with a linear timing function and an infinite iteration count

k-play-ride-seam.text: Does one full cycle end where it began?

test.spec: load the page, wait one full loop (the loop length is an open choice: 1.2, 2.4 or 4.8 s, and the wait matches the one built), then compare the first and last frames: the spokes, the crank arms and the seat sit in the same place and no part jumps

k-play-seated-ride.text: Does the rider stay seated through a stretch of the ride, with the body bobbing above the saddle?

test.spec: load the page and let it run for 10 s; sample four frames: the seat stays under the rider in each, and the torso is higher in the frames at the top of a stroke than at the bottom

k-play-reduced-and-narrow.text: Does the ride still read at a narrow width with reduced motion on?

test.spec: emulate reduced motion and a 390 px width, load the page: the bicycle and the pelican fit the frame and the pose reads at first sight

req-pelican.anchor: an SVG animation of a pelican riding a bike
req-pelican.text: The user asks for an animated SVG of a pelican riding a bicycle: motion inside one vector file, not a still picture.

principles._about: Animation principles and common mistakes that apply to a rider on a vehicle. Options, not requirements, where marked inferred.

pr-mistakes-vehicle.term: common mistakes in animated vehicles and riders
pr-mistakes-vehicle.text: The usual faults are wheels turning about the wrong center, a rider floating above the seat, feet off the pedals, and a loop that jumps at the seam.
behaviors: A wheel turning about its edge or the frame center wobbles the whole bike
Feet that do not follow the crank circle look detached
A loop whose first and last frames differ jumps at the seam
signals: wheel center off the hub
gap between seat and rider
feet not on pedal circle
frame 1 differs from frame N

pr-overlap-follow.text: Parts of the body finish at different times; the trailing part keeps moving after the main part stops.
behaviors: Parts with mass do not start or stop on the same frame
A part attached to a moving body keeps moving briefly after the body stops
pr-overlap-follow.principle: Real parts have mass and do not start or stop together.
signals: all parts arrive on the same frame
no lag between a moving body and its attached parts

pr-arcs.text: Limbs and bodies move along curved paths, not straight lines.
behaviors: Straight-line travel of a limb looks mechanical
A break in a curved path is the first thing the eye notices
pr-arcs.principle: Natural motion follows arcs, and breaks in the arc are noticed first.
signals: straight-line limb travel
linear interpolation between two poses

pr-slow-in-out.text: Motion starts and ends slowly and is fastest in the middle.
behaviors: A loop that starts and stops at constant speed looks robotic
pr-slow-in-out.principle: Weight needs time to speed up and slow down.

tokens.ease_note: ease-in-out for bob and wing; linear only for wheel rotation at constant pace

pr-anticipation-secondary.text: Anticipation is a small move before the main action; secondary action is an extra move that supports it without pulling focus.
behaviors: A small rise of the body before each pedal push makes the push read
A wing flick stays small so it does not compete with the pedaling
pr-anticipation-secondary.principle: Secondary action supports the primary action without muddying it.

motion._about: Motion of each moving piece of a pelican riding a bicycle, with timing as spreads. Derived from the primer and specifics entries; no fetched source gives cadence or wheel speed, so the timing values are illustrative.

options._about: options, not requirements: builder choices where the prompt and evidence are silent

opt-loop-length.text: Proposed loop lengths, each a whole number of wheel, crank and bob cycles so the frame at the end matches the start: 1.2 s (busy, quick), 2.4 s (steady cruise), 4.8 s (slow, relaxed).

opt-easing.term: easing of the body and wings
opt-easing.text: Two proposed easings for the bob and wings, far apart: a soft sine-like ease (gentle, cruising) and a two-step bob per stroke (punchier, more effort). Wheels and cranks stay linear in both.

mb-pivot-marked-transforms.term: SVG transform pivot shown by a red marker
mb-pivot-marked-transforms.text: Two shots mark the pivot with a red dot and outline the element with a red box; moving the dot changes where the same rotation lands.
signals: red dot marks the transform origin
red box traces the element's bounding box
one dot sits on the wordmark's letter, the other inside the mark
behaviors: Rotation turns about the dot: a wheel's pivot goes on its hub, a crank's on the bottom bracket

mo-body-bob.text: The rider and frame rise and dip once per pedal stroke as the legs push down; the saddle moves with the hips.
behaviors: The bob follows the crank: one dip per stroke, highest near the top of the push
Seat and hips move together, so the rider stays on the saddle
A small bob reads as pedaling; a large one reads as bouncing on a rough road
mo-body-bob.principle: Weight shifts with each push, so the body moves on the same beat as the cranks.

tokens.bob_per_turn: one dip per crank turn, or one per two for a looser ride

mo-wheels.text: Both wheels turn about their own hubs at the same rate, clockwise for rightward travel, while the hub stays still in the frame.
behaviors: Rotation about the hub keeps the axle still while the tyre turns
A wheel turns faster as the ride speeds up; rim speed matches ground speed
Rolling without slipping: one full turn moves the bike one tyre circumference (about 2.1 m for a 700c wheel)
A rim that drifts off the hub reads as a wobble
mo-wheels.principle: Constant rotation about the hub reads as steady riding; any drift off the hub reads as a fault.

tokens.note: 0.4 is close to real speed at about 20 km/h (about 2.6 turns per second); 1.2 reads as a slow cruise

mo-cranks.text: Crank arms turn about the bottom bracket; each pedal rides a circle around it, and each foot stays on its pedal.
behaviors: A foot that leaves the pedal circle reads as floating
The chain and rear cog turn with the cranks, so the chain moves on the pedal beat
Cranks run at constant speed, so they stay linear while the body eases
mo-cranks.principle: The feet are the one contact that matches the crank exactly.

mo-ground.text: The ground or road scrolls under the still rider, and its speed matches the wheel's rolling distance.
behaviors: Road marks move at ride speed; if they move faster than the rims, the bike seems to skate
Scroll distance per loop equals the wheel circumference times the turns per loop, or a whole multiple of the road pattern
With no road, a ground line or shadow moving left reads as motion
mo-ground.principle: Rolling without slipping ties the ground's scroll to the wheel turns.

mo-wings.text: The wings fold along the body and move in one of three sizes during a ride. Each size moves the eye a different amount, and the shoulder is the pivot at every size.
behaviors: Small, 4 to 8 deg with a cycle near 1.2 s: a tip lift on each push; the legs keep the eye and the wings stay in the background
Medium, 8 to 15 deg with a cycle of 0.8 to 1.2 s: a flap that matches the pedal beat; it reads as effort and shares the attention with the legs
Large, 15 to 25 deg with a cycle of 0.5 to 2.0 s: a wide, slow flap; it reads as gliding or lift and draws the eye to the wings
The shoulder is the pivot at every size, so the tips move further than the shoulder
mo-wings.principle: Wing size is a dial between a quiet secondary action and the main motion; the spread shows what each size does to the focus.

tokens.flap_deg: small 4 to 8, medium 8 to 15, large 15 to 25

mo-neck-bill.text: The head follows the body with a short lag and nods forward on each push. How far it moves is a dial, from almost still to a clear swing.
behaviors: Small, a nod of about 3 deg with 2 frames of lag at 30 fps: the bill barely moves and the head reads as calm
Medium, about 5 deg with 3 frames of lag: the bill tip lifts a few pixels on each push, an effort beat
Large, about 8 deg with 5 frames of lag: the neck swings forward and the bill sways with the stroke; it reads as lively and the pouch moves with it
At any size the throat pouch can sway on the nod, from none to a clear swing
mo-neck-bill.principle: The head is the far end of the body and moves last; its size sets how much of the ride the head carries.

svg_craft._about: How an animated pelican-on-bicycle SVG is built and kept working (queries 10 to 14 and 17). Techniques, not code. Either-or choices sit in the options group with their tradeoffs.

options._about: options, not requirements: either-or choices in how the motion is written, each with its tradeoffs

sc-css-vs-smil.text: Both run inside one SVG file. Pick one per file and check it in each target browser.
behaviors: CSS keyframes sit in a style block and need the origin and transform-box rules set on each rotating part
SMIL animateTransform takes the rotation centre as attribute values, so the pivot is explicit in the markup and needs no transform-box rule
SMIL timing is set per element with duration and repeat attributes, which keeps each part's timing next to the part
A media query can slow or switch off CSS motion in the same style block; SMIL cannot read that query and needs script for the same effect
sc-css-vs-smil.principle: CSS fits the page's styling and responds to viewer preferences; SMIL keeps the pivot in the markup and works where the style block is unavailable.
signals: pivot missing on a CSS part
animation ignores the reduced-motion query

sc-reduced-motion.text: Less-motion viewers can get a version that moves less and still reads as a pelican on a bike. The k-reduced-motion check asks for wheels stopped or slowed; unchanged does not meet it.
options: stopped: wheels and cranks hold still and the pose carries the picture; the bike, rider and bill need to read with no motion
slowed: every part keeps the same shape on a longer cycle, so the wheels turn more slowly
unchanged: the wheels keep their full-speed turn and only the body bob and wing movement is dropped
behaviors: Stopping leaves a still picture, so the bike, rider and bill need to read clearly with no motion
Dropping the bob and wings keeps the sense of travel with the least movement near the eye
sc-reduced-motion.principle: Motion that cannot be turned off can cause discomfort for people with vestibular disorders.
signals: no reduced-motion rule in the file
pose unreadable when the ride stops

sv-pivot-per-part.text: Set transform-origin on each rotating part: each wheel's hub, the crank center on the bottom bracket, and the wing shoulder. Parts that do not rotate, such as the frame and the body, need none.
behaviors: Each wheel turns about its own hub; the frame and rider move with the bike, not with the wheel's rim
sv-pivot-per-part.principle: Only the element that turns needs a pivot; setting it on a parent group moves every child with it.
signals: hub stays fixed in the frame
rim turns while hub holds

tokens.hub: a point at the center of the wheel's own box

sc-groups.text: Build the drawing as nested groups: ground and background at the back, then wheels, frame and cranks, then the rider's body, neck, bill and wings in front.
behaviors: Each wheel is its own group that turns about its hub while the frame group carries the rest of the bike
Moving a parent group moves every child, so the rider group rolls with the frame
Layer order decides which part hides which: the rear wheel sits behind the frame and the legs sit over the front wheel
sc-groups.principle: Each moving part gets one group with one pivot, and the hierarchy carries motion down to the parts.
signals: wheel drifting away from the frame
legs drawn over the front wheel by mistake

sc-self-contained.text: The whole animation lives in one SVG document with its style embedded; nothing outside the file is referenced.
behaviors: Any external stylesheet, script, font or image breaks the file when it is opened alone or embedded as an image
Text in a font the viewer lacks falls back to another face, so convert labels to outlines to keep the drawing fixed
An SVG used as an image element plays its animation but runs no scripts, so timing must live in the file's own style or timing markup
sc-self-contained.principle: A drawing that carries everything it needs plays the same wherever it is opened.
signals: external URL in the file
font-dependent label

sc-loop-seam.text: A loop repeats without a jump only when every animated part ends in the state it started in.
behaviors: A wheel that turns a full revolution, or an even fraction of one, lands on the same spokes at the seam
A bob that goes down and back up within the cycle has matching ends; a bob that stops halfway snaps at the repeat
Parts with different cycle lengths loop together only when each cycle divides the full loop length
sc-loop-seam.principle: The seam is checked part by part; a picture can look right while one part snaps.
signals: visible snap at the repeat
spokes shifting at the repeat

sc-performance.text: Keep the moving parts few and move them by transform and opacity, so the browser shifts groups without repainting the drawing.
behaviors: Rotating a wheel group is one transform per frame; changing path data every frame repaints the path
A handful of animated groups stays smooth; animating the shape of every path does not
Opacity on a group can add a blink or a shadow without touching the paths inside it
sc-performance.principle: Few moving parts, each moved by transform, is the cheap way to make a ride look busy.
signals: stutter on a phone
path shape attribute animated

sv-pivot.text: The transform origin is the point a rotation is applied around; CSS centers it by default, and transform-box sets what a percentage is measured against.
behaviors: Moving the origin changes where a rotation lands, even when the angle is the same
With transform-box: fill-box and transform-origin: 50% 50%, a wheel rotates about its own center
sv-pivot.principle: The origin is part of the transform; a rotation without it turns about the wrong point.
signals: same angle, different place
transform-box missing on a rotating group
quotes: The object bounding box is used as the reference box.

sv-loop-reduced-motion.text: A loop closes when the keyframes at 0% and 100% match; prefers-reduced-motion asks for less non-essential motion.
behaviors: A wheel or crank whose end angle differs from its start angle jumps at the seam
Under reduce, a large body bob or scroll can be slowed or stopped while the ride stays readable
sv-loop-reduced-motion.principle: Motion that cannot be turned off can cause discomfort for people with vestibular disorders.
quotes: Such animations can trigger discomfort for those with vestibular motion disorders.
signals: 0% and 100% keyframes differ
no prefers-reduced-motion block
pose unreadable when the ride stops

sc-viewbox-scale.text: Draw once on a fixed coordinate space and let the element scale to the width of the page. The viewBox shape is a choice between a wide, short box and a 4:3 box, each with what it does.
behaviors: 1000 by 600 (wide and short): the bike and rider sit side by side with room above for the bill; on a phone the scene becomes a short band and the bill and pouch get small
800 by 600 (4:3): taller in proportion, so the rider and bike fill more of the frame and the bill and pouch keep more height on a phone; a wide, short box gives more room to the side
Setting the width to the container and letting the height follow the aspect gives a phone and a desktop the same composition
sc-viewbox-scale.principle: Compose for the viewBox once; scaling is free only if nothing sits outside it.
signals: bill clipped at the top edge
wheels cut at the bottom edge

pelican_and_bicycle._about: Drawable parts for a pelican seated on a bicycle, side view. Proportions are illustrative spreads, not sourced ratios. Layer order, back to front: far wheel, far pedal and foot, frame, chain, saddle, pelican body, far wing, near wing, legs and feet, neck and head, bars, near wheel. Options, not requirements, are in the options group. Drawn coordinates (the silhouettes, the bicycle parts' positions and the bottom bracket's viewBox point) are set in the draw step, not here: this section gives parts and proportions, not coordinates, and the write route takes its coordinates from the draw step.

options._about: options, not requirements: layouts for each reading of the rider's position

opt-saddle-layout.text: Tail over the saddle with the rump on the seat; belly over the saddle with the body hanging lower; or tail over the rear wheel, which lengthens the body line.

tokens.body_drop_below_saddle: 0 to a third of body length

opt-handlebar-layout.text: Wing tips on the grips, which keeps the reach readable; wings spread wide for balance with no grip; or the whole bird perched on the bars with feet on a cradle, not the pedals.

tokens.grip_reach: wing tip to bar, short to long

ps-pelican-recognize.text: Up close the bill and throat pouch identify a pelican; at distance the long bill and chunky body read first.
behaviors: A pouch that hangs below the lower jaw makes the head read as a pelican before any other detail does
ps-pelican-recognize.principle: The pouch and bill are the single largest identifiers; keep them legible at small size.
signals: pouch hangs below the jaw
bill longer than the head

ps-rider-contact.text: Three contacts hold the rider: saddle, two pedals, and bars. Saddle height is set from the bottom bracket.
behaviors: Saddle height is measured to the middle of the bottom bracket, so the seat sits at a fixed distance above the crank center
Inseam times 0.883 gives bottom-bracket-to-saddle height (LeMond), which ignores crank length
ps-rider-contact.principle: The seat and pedal path decide how the body moves; keep both fixed to the frame.
signals: seat stays on saddle through the loop
foot follows the pedal circle

ps-viewer-checks.text: A viewer checks that each wheel spins on its hub, each foot stays on its pedal circle, and the seat stays under the rider.
behaviors: A rim that drifts off the hub reads as a wobble
A foot that leaves the pedal circle reads as floating
ps-viewer-checks.principle: Contact points are what make a cartoon ride believable at small size.
signals: foot path is a circle
hub stays fixed in the frame

ragged long primary feathers at the wingtips
head and neck short, bill hard to read at this size
body a small dark mass where the wings join
behaviors: A straight dark wing bar with drooping tips identifies the pelican before the bill does

mb-bicycle-silhouette.text: A side-on road bike reads from two equal wheel rings and a sloping frame triangle.
signals: two equal wheel rings, the largest shapes
top tube sloping down to a low head tube

drop handlebar at the front
bottom bracket under the frame between the wheels

mb-crank-and-contact-layout.term: crank, chainring and seat contact at the bottom bracket
mb-crank-and-contact-layout.text: The crank center sits in the frame below the seat tube, and the saddle is the rider's seat contact on a straight seatpost.
signals: chainring and crank arm seen from the drive side
rear hub and wheel beside the bottom bracket
saddle on a straight seatpost, the seat point
behaviors: A pedal turns about the crank center, not about the wheel hub; the seat stays in fixed contact with the body

pb-pelican-legs-feet.text: Short legs set back under the body, with webbed feet that rest on the pedals; the visible joint that looks like a knee is the ankle.
behaviors: The hip is hidden under the body; the thigh swings about it and the shin bends at the visible ankle
The foot rests on the pedal at the ball of the foot and follows the pedal circle
pb-pelican-legs-feet.principle: Hip and saddle stay fixed to the frame; the feet move on the pedal circle, so draw the feet on that path.

toes over the pedal axle

pb-rider-contacts.text: Four contacts hold the pelican to the bike: the seat under the body, two feet on the pedals, and one wing tip on a grip.
behaviors: Each contact stays on its anchor part; the feet move on the pedal circle and the seat stays put
A body bob moves the seat contact in step with the seat, so no gap opens between rump and saddle
pb-rider-contacts.principle: Attach each contact to its anchor, so a moving part keeps its support.
signals: no gap between rump and saddle
foot circle centered on the crank

ps-bicycle-parts.text: A diamond frame with two wheels, cranks at the bottom bracket, a saddle on the seat post and bars on the head tube; sizes vary by bike.
behaviors: Each wheel turns about its own hub; the frame rides along and does not rotate
Crank arms and chainring turn about the bottom bracket, the center of the pedal circle
The chainring and rear cog turn in a fixed ratio, so the rear wheel turns faster than the cranks
Saddle and bars stay fixed to the frame, so the body moves against them
ps-bicycle-parts.principle: Wheels and cranks are the pivots; the frame is the rigid link that carries the rider.
signals: wheel center is the hub
pedal circle centered on bottom bracket
spokes sweep
frame stays level

pb-pelican-head.text: A long flat bill, a pouch hanging from the lower jaw, and a short S-curved neck that carries the head forward of the chest.
behaviors: The pouch hangs below the jaw, so the head reads as a pelican before any other detail does
Tilting the head changes the bill angle more than bending the neck does
Exact ratios vary by species; pick one species silhouette and keep it
pb-pelican-head.principle: The bill and pouch identify the bird at small size and carry the expression.
signals: pouch visible under the bill
bill longer than the head
neck curve reads as an S

pb-pelican-body-wing.text: A long flattened body with the wing folded along its side, hinged at a shoulder joint near the front of the back.

behaviors: The wing turns about the shoulder, not about its tip, so the whole wing swings as one piece

pv-svg-default-origin.text: An SVG child element's transform-origin defaults to (0,0) of the viewBox, not to the element's own center, so a part rotates around the wrong point unless the pivot is set.

lx-pelican.text: The seabird Pelecanus, drawn as a chunky cartoon with a long bill and a hanging throat pouch.
associations: Nigel, the pelican in Finding Nemo: a deadpan cartoon pelican

lx-bike.text: A pedal bicycle: two wheels, a diamond frame, a chain driven by cranks, a saddle and bars.
associations: Bicycle Thieves (1948): a bicycle as the whole story
penny-farthing: a tall front wheel, a deep cut in cartoon shorthand
a cargo bike with a box in front: a ready-made gag prop

lx-riding.text: Seated on the saddle, pedaling and leaning into turns; the rider moves as one body with the frame.
associations: a pelican perched on the bars: the second reading, a balance gag
coasting with wings out: a glide played as a gag
a slow leisure ride along a shore: a ground-level scene

lx-animation.text: Motion built from keyframes, timing and easing, here inside one SVG file that loops or plays on load.
associations: walk cycle: a repeating limb pose at a constant period
hold frames: a pose kept still for beats, the cartoon pause
smear frame: a blurred streak in fast motion
flipbook: the oldest cycle, a sense of frame rate
